title: Trying a New Approach
keyIdea: If the way you are trying is not working, doing it again the same way usually gives the same result. Good learners notice this and switch to a new approach: draw it, break it into parts, work backwards, or ask how someone else did it. Then they check which way worked better, so they can use it next time.

kid: A robot walks into a wall. Bump! It tries again the same way. Bump! Doing the same thing again gives the same result.
So try a new way. Go round the wall. Draw a picture of the sum. Break a long word into small parts. Start at the end and work backwards.
Switching is not giving up. You are still trying. You are just trying in a smarter way.
Then check. Which way worked better? Remember it. Next time you can use the best way first.
adult: Psychologists call this cognitive flexibility, or strategy switching. It is part of metacognition: planning how to tackle a task, monitoring whether it is working, and evaluating the result. The Education Endowment Foundation guidance on metacognition and self-regulated learning (2018) uses this plan, monitor, evaluate cycle. It recommends that teachers model it out loud. Repeating a failed method with more effort is called perseveration. Children of 7 and 8 are still learning to stop it.

In the US, Common Core Mathematical Practice 1, make sense of problems and persevere in solving them, says students monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. It also says they try special cases and simpler forms of the problem. In England, the national curriculum aims for mathematics ask pupils to solve problems, including breaking them down into simpler steps. At Year 2 they use concrete objects and pictures to solve problems. The same idea applies in spelling: when sounding out fails on a common exception word such as friend, a child needs another strategy.

Common mistakes: trying the same method harder or faster, as when a child recounts a muddle of objects one by one and gets a new total each time. Believing that changing method is giving up or cheating. Sticking with the first idea because it was theirs. Swapping methods at random without checking which one worked. Be careful not to hand over the new method straight away. Ask "Is this way working? What else could you try?" first.

In the lab your child steers a robot that bumps a wall until they find a new route, and counts 23 stars by grouping in fives after Ben's one-by-one counts failed. They sort ideas into same again or new approach, and match problems to draw it, break it into parts or work backwards. Then they judge which of two tries worked better.

familyTip: When your child gets stuck, ask "Is this way working?" before you help. Keep a short family list of new ways to try, such as draw it, break it up, work backwards, or ask how someone else did it. When a new way works, ask "Which way was better, and why?"

visual.caption: Same thing again, or a new approach? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Read the page again at the same speed
Kick the ball at the same spot again
Copy the same answer out neatly
Make it a smaller problem first

lab.caption: Flagship lab: steer a robot round a wall, count stars a new way, sort same again from new approach, pick a strategy, and judge which way worked.

practice.prompt: Ava tried a sum 3 times the same way and got it wrong each time. What should she do?
choices: Try a new way, like drawing it
practice.hint: Will the same way give a different answer this time?
practice.explain: The same way gave the same wrong answer 3 times. Drawing it is a new approach that might show her the slip.

practice.prompt: Sam puts his buttons in groups of 5. He makes {n} full groups. How many buttons is that?
practice.hint: Count on in fives, once for each of the {n} groups.
practice.explain: {n} groups of 5 is {=5*n}. Counting in fives was quicker than one by one.

practice.prompt: Which one is a new approach to spelling a long word?
practice.hint: Which one changes how you try, not how hard?
practice.explain: Breaking a word into parts, like foot + ball, is a new way. The others repeat the same way.

practice.prompt: Mo had some stickers. He gave away 4, and now he has {n}. Work backwards: how many did he have at the start?
practice.hint: Start at the end with {n}, then put back the 4 he gave away.
practice.explain: {n} add the 4 he gave away is {=n+4}. Working backwards from the end solved it.

pool.prompt: Is trying a new approach the same as giving up?
choices: No. You are still trying, in a new way.
pool.hint: When you switch ways, are you still working on the problem?
pool.explain: Switching to a new way keeps you working on the problem. Giving up would mean stopping.

pool.prompt: A door will not open when you push it. What is a new approach?
pool.hint: Pushing harder is still pushing. What else could you do with a door?
pool.explain: Pulling is a different move. Pushing harder or again is the same way.

pool.prompt: A new way worked better than your first way. What should you do next time?
choices: Remember it and try it first
pool.hint: Checking which way worked helps you choose next time.
pool.explain: Remembering the way that worked saves time on the next problem like it.

pool.prompt: A shop has 4 shelves with 3 toys on each. Which strategy helps most?
choices: Break the word shop into parts
pool.hint: Can you picture the shelves and the toys?
pool.explain: Drawing 4 shelves with 3 toys each lets you see and count all 12 toys.

pool.prompt: Ben counted a big pile of shells one by one and got a different answer each time. Why?
choices: One by one is easy to lose count
pool.hint: Think of Ben and the stars in the lab.
pool.explain: In a muddle it is easy to skip one or count one twice. Groups of 5 or 10 help.

pool.prompt: You count marbles in groups of 10. You make {n} full groups and have 3 left over. How many marbles?
pool.hint: Count in tens for the {n} groups, then count on 3.
pool.explain: {n} tens is {=10*n}, and 3 more makes {=10*n+3}. Groups of 10 made it quick.

pool.prompt: You cannot read the word “rainbow”. Which new approach helps?
pool.hint: Can you see two small words hiding in it?
pool.explain: Rain + bow are two words you know. Breaking it into parts makes it easy to read.

pool.prompt: Some birds were on a wall. {n} more came. Now there are {=n+5}. Work backwards: how many were there at first?
pool.hint: Start at the end and take away the {n} birds that came.
pool.explain: {=n+5} take away {n} is 5. Working backwards found the start.

pool.prompt: You tried two ways. Way 1 got the wrong answer. Way 2 got it right. Which worked better?
pool.hint: Look at the results, not which way you tried first.
pool.explain: Way 2 got the right answer, so it worked better. Checking results helps you choose.
